debate_title: AI governance frameworks for advanced AI systems

conflicts.point: Whether upstream training compute thresholds ($10^{26}$ integer operations) effectively prevent downstream operational bias and systemic risks at the inference layer.

positions.stance: Argues that scaling compute creates distinct systemic risks that justify targeting developers above the $10^{26}$ threshold with pre-deployment audits.
Maintains that static upstream training compute thresholds fail to track dynamic fine-tuned behaviors and leave downstream inference bias unaddressed.

conflicts.point: Whether tiered safe harbor provisions and compute-indexed audits adequately protect open-source and smaller developers from prohibitive regulatory compliance costs.

positions.stance: Claims that tiered safe harbors and exemptions for sub-threshold builders successfully shield garage developers from administrative friction.
Asserts that software supply chain dependencies mean downstream users of base models still inherit compliance burdens, making fixed costs prohibitive regardless of nominal exemptions.

verdicts.conflict: Whether upstream training compute thresholds ($10^{26}$ integer operations) effectively prevent downstream operational bias and systemic risks at the inference layer.
verdicts.rationale: Both positions track valid dimensions of a complex technical reality. The safetyist position correctly identifies that base model scale creates immutable systemic baselines, while the accelerationist position correctly notes that fine-tuning alters downstream behavior in ways static compute counts fail to capture.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Longitudinal empirical tracking of model failures showing whether pre-deployment audits catch more systemic harms than post-deployment behavioral monitoring.

verdicts.conflict: Whether tiered safe harbor provisions and compute-indexed audits adequately protect open-source and smaller developers from prohibitive regulatory compliance costs.
verdicts.rationale: The skeptic position provides concrete operational details regarding recurring third-party audit costs and cryptographic logging requirements. The safetyist counter-argument relies on nominal exemptions that fail to account for software supply chain inheritance where downstream users depend on upstream base models.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Empirical cost-accounting studies of compliance expenses across startup cohorts indicating whether safe harbors successfully preserve open-source market entry.
